name: Zero-Based Budgeting
title: Zero-Based Budgeting
answer: Zero-based budgeting is a planning method in which every cost line starts at zero and must be justified for the coming period, rather than being carried forward from last year's figure with an adjustment. In finance teams it sits alongside forecasting and variance analysis as a way of rebuilding the cost base from the activity up. It applies most often to discretionary spend, overheads and shared services, where the link between money and output is loose enough to invite challenge. The method is a budgeting discipline first and a software category second, though most large deployments now run inside a planning platform.

sections.body: Zero-based budgeting is a planning method in which every cost line starts at zero and must be justified for the coming period, rather than being carried forward from last year's figure with an adjustment. In finance teams it sits alongside forecasting and variance analysis as a way of rebuilding the cost base from the activity up. It applies most often to discretionary spend, overheads and shared services, where the link between money and output is loose enough to invite challenge. The method is a budgeting discipline first and a software category second, though most large deployments now run inside a planning platform.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: The work runs on a planning or enterprise performance management system that holds the chart of accounts, cost centres, headcount and vendor records, with a calculation engine that rolls activity up into cost. Data arrives from the general ledger, the HR system, procurement and contract repositories, usually through scheduled extracts rather than manual entry. Spreadsheets still carry a large share of the modelling in smaller organisations, which is where version control and audit trail problems tend to start. Access is normally role based, so a cost centre owner sees only their own build and finance sees the consolidated view.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: Practitioners break the organisation into decision units, define the activities each unit performs, and cost those activities from the ground up using drivers such as transaction volume, headcount or service level. Each unit then submits a set of packages at different funding levels, and reviewers rank them so that a constrained budget can be assembled from the top down. Machine learning enters mainly at the edges, for example classifying ledger entries, flagging anomalous spend or forecasting volumes that feed the activity drivers. The output is a cost base tied to stated service levels, which makes trade-offs visible in a way that incremental budgeting does not.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Because zero-based budgeting asks managers to defend their own spend, the process needs clear ownership of decision units, documented assumptions and a review trail that shows who approved which package. Provenance matters here: every driver figure should trace back to a source system or a named estimate, and the version that was approved should be distinguishable from later revisions. Where automated classification or anomaly detection touches financial data, the usual controls apply, including access logging, retention rules and review of model outputs before they affect a reported number.Nothing in this description is legal, financial or investment advice.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: The direction of travel is toward continuous zero-based review rather than an annual rebuild, with driver data refreshed monthly and packages re-ranked as volumes move. Planning vendors are folding classification, forecasting and natural language query into the same platform, which shortens the gap between a submitted package and a challenge to it. The persistent difficulty is behavioural rather than technical, since the method only works if managers accept the scrutiny and reviewers resist the temptation to pad. Expect more automation of the mechanical parts and continued debate about how much of the judgement can be delegated to a model.
